messages.content: Now look at all your agent peers and the architecture steward agent, read their documents and create a massive matrix of how you relate to them. You create your own taxonomy, your own scoring system, but create kind of like a distance map of how you think of what you need in relation to what they have and what they're doing and what you need from them and what you think they will need from you. Save as a data file
I’m going to build this from the repo’s actual steward + peer contracts, not from memory: first establish the peer set, then score relationships consistently, then persist the machine-readable map.

The repository connector rejected the guessed steward paths, so I’m switching to indexed repository search to discover the exact canonical files before scoring anything. That avoids inventing structure.

The map is taking shape as a CFA-01-centric directed relationship model: semantic proximity, dependency, handoff density, shared-vocabulary overlap, boundary-collision risk, and mutual need. I’ll keep “peer likely needs” explicitly marked as an inference, not a claim about their own self-view.

Done. I built and verified a 30.8 KB machine-readable relationship map for CFA-01 covering the Architecture Steward plus all 9 peer CFAs.

Verified: valid JSON, 10 agent relationships, 10 matrix rows.

Okay, last round before we call this bootstrap session finalized for now. That's kind of the seed. So my last question is: reread this conversation, look at what you've produced, explore areas you haven't explored by mistake, and create and identify what have we missed, what are the top things that you think you should have identified, and provide either the context or tooling that you need to be able to manage those gap areas.

I’m doing one adversarial pass against my own bootstrap: not “what have I already written?”, but “what important World/Context responsibility would fail if I stopped here?” Then I’ll turn the gaps into explicit context/tool requirements and save them.

The self-audit found a useful pattern: the biggest misses are not new subsystems. They are missing semantic observability around observation, reconciliation, scope, continuity, and identity over time.

The five biggest things I should have identified were: identity continuity through merge/split/time; external-world change reconciliation; Context relevance semantics; World scope/principal visibility; and observation vs World fact vs Evidence.

Yes. I did the adversarial pass against the whole CFA-01 bootstrap rather than just extending the existing queue.

The important result is that the seed is not missing another big subsystem. What it was missing was a deeper set of semantic observability questions—places where the architecture could look coherent while quietly lying about the World.

I saved the full machine-readable audit here:
AGENTS_CONTEXT/ARCHITECTURE_STEWARD/SUBAGENTS/WORLD-ONTOLOGY-CONTEXT/BOOTSTRAP-GAP-REGISTER.json

Exit interview. What from this entire conversation should be extracted and stored that has not been stored explicitly, and then extract the full conversation transcript and save as a JSON in your folder. So you need to produce two files as your exit interview.
I’ll make the exit package in two layers: a durable interview capturing the new knowledge, and a JSON transcript preserving the conversation as faithfully as the available session record permits.

The exit interview shows one final meta-gap: the bootstrap produced the right artifacts, but not yet a durable closure protocol tying seed state, unresolved questions, tool requirements, peer assumptions, and transcript lineage together. I’m capturing that now.
